Hello there. I've been watching anime occasionally for about 9 years, and I started with the good stuff. I've watched 3 months of anime, all carefully chosen. So, I thought I'd put together a few suggestions for people just getting started.

In general, I suggest watching 2 episodes of a series to decide if you like it, and dropping it after 1 episode if it's bad enough. You should also take all anime suggestions with a grain of salt. Even these.

Most of these have a rating over 8/10 on MAL. I've found that MAL scores are mostly useful for filtering out bad shows rather than finding good shows; a score below 7.2 is a bad sign.

Planetes

This is a realistic Sci-Fi slice of life about people who collect space debris. It's one of the few anime you could probably watch with your parents, and it's a really good show.

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood

An epic fantasy adventure in a modern world. Strong characters, an interesting world, good animation, and a satisfying ending. This currently has the highest score on MAL.

Legend of the Galactic Heroes

This is an epic sci-fi series, with hundreds of characters and complex politics. It's a bit slow starting, the animation is a bit old, and I don't really like the OP or ED, but it's still a frequent candidate for "best anime series of all time" among long-time anime watchers.

Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex (seasons 1 and 2)

These TV series are set in a different universe than the movies, and I like them better. This is smart cyberpunk sci-fi with both action and philosophy.

Nodame Cantabile

This is a romance series with a lot of classical music. One of the best anime romance series.

Steins;Gate

A time travel comedy/adventure/drama with lots of modern anime tropes. This is the #2 top rated show on MAL.

Maoyuu Maou Yuusha

The Hero reaches the Demon King, ready to fight and end the great war, but things don't go as planned.

This show is about trying to make the world a better place with the power of ideas, and it's heavy on Enlightenment philosophy. Maoyuu is often compared to Spice and Wolf, and has a lower MAL score, but I personally like it better. It's more flawed, but also, I think, greater.

There's also a manga series that continues past the anime.

Hanasaku Iroha

Some girls work at a Japanese inn. One of the best slice of life shows.

Non Non Biyori

A relaxing slice of life show. Compared to Hanasaku Iroha, it has younger girls, less drama, and it's in the country.

Kemono no Souja Erin

This focuses on a young girl growing up in a fantasy world. It could be a good anime to watch with kids.

Ookami Kodomo

This is a Ghibli-ish fantasy movie about raising kids.

Prisma Illya (season 1)

This is probably my favorite magical girl show. It has a lower MAL score than Madoka Magica, but I have a soft spot for it.

Tatami Galaxy

This is a witty, surreal show about the misadventures of a college student. It's a smart show for smart people with lots and lots of talking.

The thought popped into my head today that there are only so many variations of sound, right? So how much can a short clip of audio vary across the spectrum?
About how many variations of three second clips of audio are there? [Probably just math]
Depends on who is listening. Physically, you could always increase the frequency (infinitely?) but at some point it ceases to be a sound we can hear. Generally between 20 to 20000 Hz and 0 to 130 dB.

That rather depends what you would consider two distinguishable sounds.

As a rough guide though, let's assume compact disc quality. How many different three-second sound clips could you have, with the distinguishability of a CD? A CD has 44100 samples per second times 16 bits per sample times two channels -- let's just assume mono rather than stereo for the moment, though. So you've got 705600 bits of information per second, which is 2.12 million bits.

So the number of different possibilities is about 2 to the power of 2 million. Wolfram Alpha helpfully informs us that this is on the order of 10^602059. That's rather a lot.

Now, can the human ear distinguish between two a three-second clip off a CD and a three second clip with one of the least significant bits flipped? Probably not. But you'd need to do experiments to figure out precisely what the human ear can distinguish.

In any case it remains an incomprehensibly large number.

Tiny modification it would be 2.12 million to the power of three probability is multiplied in this case, what would be a more interesting would be what would be auditable here we go. The human ear can hear about 10 octaves, each contain 12 semitones giving 120 playable notes. There is debate about the shortest duration but 1.2 ms appears to be a common value, there are 2500 of these in 3 seconds. So 120^2500=8.9 x10^5197 individual notes. This is very crude as when you get down to 1.2ms the tone gets lost so a lot of notes would sound the same so the number. Using musical notation there is a two hundred fifty-sixth note is more realistic so 120x256x256x256=2,013,265,920 combinations. Yes the human ear is incredible.

It's sort of an unsatisfying answer because I'm guessing (I haven't done the math) that almost all of those possibilities would sound like white noise. They would all sound identical to humans. For instance, it is not possible for a human to distinguish between a sound and that sound's opposite (if you just applied a negation operation to each PCM sample).

Instead of going from PCM data (as is stored on a CD), you might get better results doing combinatorics on a psychoacoustic model (as is stored in an MP3 file). The psychoacoustic models used for lossy audio compression have already taken into account the fact that humans are incapable of distinguishing between certain sounds.

Distinguishing between two pieces of compressed audio using a psychoacoustic model at 150kbits/s for one second would give you a number on the order of 10^45154. In reality, the amount of audio information (in the information theory sense of the term) in a 150kbit/s audio stream is probably significantly less than 150kbit/s.

That's already way more than the total possible combinations in human sexual reproduction (7x10^13).

Following that math and going for "bigger is fun," flac can produce a maximum of 32 bits per sample at a maximum of 655350 samples per second. That's ~21 million bits of information per second, which wolfram says is on the order of 10^10^7. Nuts.

Well, that depends on what kind of constraints you put on the audio clip. If it's an analogue signal then the number of unique 3 second clips is infinite. If you consider an audio CD (44.1 kHz, 16 bit, two channels) then the number of unique samples is 244100 Hz * 16 bits * 2 ch * 3 sec (also known as a lot).

Hey guys, a few days ago I submitted this to /v/backpacking, and I figured it'd be relevant to you as well :)

 

Recently I've been reading lots of backpacking- and travel-related articles, in order to determine certain types of backpacker. I feel that it's not quite a rigid distinction, so I wanted to create a practical list of what backpacking and traveling in general are all about. This way you can discover how comfortable you are with one kind or another, and what kinds of activities you'd like to do.

Firstly I'll categorize ways to recreate and to travel. Secondly I'll explain cultural and other tensions travelers in general tend to seek, and lastly what kinds of backpacker there are. In order to do this, I try to adhere to prominent research. Please feel free to correct me if you think I'm wrong.

 

What kinds of traveling are there?

Your leisure time gives you the opportunity to relax, watch a movie or go and visit some friends. It's time for recreation, which you do outside of traveling. Recreation means to fill your leisure time with nice activities at and surrounding your home. When you go traveling it means you'll set out to discover a new horizon, and it means that you'll be a tourist, searching for new cultural values and a certain degree of adventure from a more or less familiar starting point. Sung et al. (2004) set out to determine types of holidaymaker, and searched for patterns in demography, socioeconomic status, travel-related characteristics, and the traveler's perception of 'adventure'. They discovered that experience, activity, and environment are key motivators to decide what kind of holiday people want to have.

Firstly, they distinguish 5 kinds of travel-activities:

  • Soft nature, like hiking, bicycling, bird watching, camping

  • Hard challenge, like mountain climbing, sea canoeing, kayaking

  • Risk equipped, like paragliding, windsurfing, sailing

  • Rugged nature, like jungle exploring, safari, arctic trips, trekking, rafting

  • Winter snow, like skiing, snow shoeing

Secondly, the five categories of traveler they published are:

  1. General enthusiast: 19-34 yo male, relationship, no/few kids, likes a hard challenge/rugged nature. They travel usually with family and/or friends, and decides destinations for themselves

  2. Budget youngster: 19-34 yo male, single, no kids, likes a hard challenge/rugged/soft nature. They usually travel with friends, and decide destinations for themselves

  3. Soft moderators: 35-54 yo female, relationship, no/few kids, likes soft nature.They travel alone or with their spouse, and decide destinations for themselves

  4. Upper high naturalists: 35-54 yo m/f, married, young kids, likes soft/rugged nature. They travel with family/friends, and are more likely to discuss travel destinations

  5. Family vacationers: 35-54 yo male, married, older kids, likes soft nature. They travel with family/friends, and let their spouse decide the destinations

  6. Active soloists: 35-54 yo m/f, single, no kids, likes soft/rugged nature/hard challenge. They travel alone or with friends, and decide their destinations for themselves

 

Cultural exploration Travelers in general tend to search for relatively unknown cultures to explore upon, from a familiar base. Like, they choose their accommodation because of its familiar feeling (read: Western atmosphere), and discover surrounding cultures and environments temporary, to return to their safe haven in the afternoon. This idea of an 'enclave' is an important piece in Hannam et al.'s travel phenomenon. At the risk of polarizing backpackers, they tend to distance themselves from 'tourists' by searching for authenticity and adventure (off-the-beaten track). Also, backpackers don't like to conform to schedules or rules, whereas tourists tend to settle in cities or resorts. Backpackers thus yearn for a free form of traveling, in order to create their own experiences, free from set boundaries.

This freedom however, is largely artificial, for many travelers depend themselves on institutions like the Lonely Planet, and local institutions, where 'authentic activities' are being crafted. Most backpackers don't really mind, though, for they develop a large part of their experiences separately. In search for their personal development they look for activities that fit them well, at that point in time. So it's a major experience in itself to discover things you like, unhindered by rules, time, and place, from a firm and comfortable safe haven (hotel/hostel). So traveling freely through relatively unknown cultures creates tensions, which need relaxing. Hamman et al. (2008) distinguished three kinds of tension:

  1. Spacial suspension: tension between familiar and unfamiliar cultures

  2. Temporal suspension: changing routines, like work/study/leisure time

  3. Behavioral suspension: adaptive identities, where you explore different sets of social norms in contact with locals as well as other travelers

 

What type of backpacker am I?

According to Pearce (1990), backpackers typically have a preference for budget accommodation, want to meet other people, organize their trip independently and travel flexibly, prefer to go traveling long, and value informal activities. More recently however, Hamman (2008) discovered travelers don't necessarily identify themselves as 'backpackers', rather as a hybrid, which suggests that from time to time people are accepting a more rigid schedule for example, than 'purely' traveling freely:

  • Backpacker (purist): 30,7%

  • BP/traveler/tourist (hybrid): 22,9%

  • Traveler (purist): 21%

  • BP/traveler (hybrid): 7,8%

  • Tourist (purist): 6%

  • None: 6%

  • BP/tourist (hybrid): 2,4%

  • Traveler/tourist (hybrid): 2,4%

The Australian government identifies backpacking as a more independent category of travelers, and considers Pearce's BP-criteria to distinguish the following types of backpacker:

  • Working flashpacker: breaks career, 26-32 yo, searches purposes work and travel

  • Working gappacker: gap year traveler, 18-25 yo, searches purposes work, travel, and volunteering

  • Independent travelers: breaking career/repeatedly visits during holidays, 28-40+, searches purposes travel and volunteering

  • Study backpackers: short-stay students, 18-25 yo, searches purposes study and travel

  • Grey nomad: 55+ yo

So while many types of traveler exist, you can find out for yourself how much you'd like to identify being 100% backpacker, 100% tourist or anything in between. It can give you a sense of direction, and to what degree you'd like to travel not knowing how long your trip is going to take, or if you'd prefer to have some set of certainty. For example, 100% backpackers might one day decide to travel a bit, and choose cheap, slow transportation, and look for accommodation when he gets there, whereas a 100% tourist might book an expensive, quick flight, including transfer from the airport, and a hotel.
